meaning: Titles and reading notes drafted by an AI agent in the register of the paper they annotate. No mathematician has reviewed them.

notes.PCP.Algebraic.BLR.exists_linearMap_dista: For any Boolean-valued function on a finite binary vector space, rejection probability at most $\epsilon$ in the linearity test guarantees a linear functional within distance $\epsilon$. No small-error threshold is imposed. The conclusion is linearity as a function of the input vector; it does not yet identify a Hadamard word as evaluation at a field element. In the Hadamard test, the unit and product conditions supply that additional identification.
Let the selected column positions be distinct, with column polynomials of degree at most $D$. Suppose more than $(d+2e+2)D$ parameter values admit a degree-$d$ row polynomial with at most $e$ discrepancies, and there are more than $d+e$ selected columns. Then the statement constructs $E\ne0$ and $N$ satisfying all column identities, with degrees in the first variable at most $e$ and $d+e$, and in the second at most $(d+2e+1)D$. Here the paper uses $e=2d$ and $D=d$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryDifferenceConsistenc: Replacing the colour table and the difference table can increase the difference check’s rejection probability by at most twice the colour-table distance plus once the difference-table distance. Both distances are measured over homogeneous labels. The factor two occurs because the check reads the colour table at each endpoint. The replacements may be arbitrary tables; they need not be polynomial encodings. When each distance is at most $\varepsilon$, the loss is at most $3\varepsilon$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.fail: For each target $a$, assume the points table is within homogeneous-label distance $\delta$ of a polynomial $P$ with $\deg P\le D$ and $D\ge cb^c$. With $q>2c$, generator test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes, the probability of rejection or an incorrect bit is at most $C_c\kappa_a+\delta+D/[2(q-1)]$. The lines table is arbitrary. This bound averages over the homogeneous label and gives no independent upper bound on the corrector’s own rejection probability $\kappa_a$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.quer: The local corrector’s complete query list has length at most $3c+9$ for every supplied sample. It includes the inner low-degree test, the comparison with the points table and both corrected reads of the line entry. The bound does not assume honest tables, generator nodes or a large field. Correctness on honest encodings is proved separately, so this statement should be tied to the first sentence of the quoted passage.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run: For a fixed target and supplied random choices, the procedure first tests the selected line entry. It then compares a corrected bit of that entry at the nonzero line parameter with a bit of the points table. If either check fails it rejects; otherwise it returns the corrected bit at parameter zero. The two corrections use the same inner slope and homogeneous label. This definition supplies the procedure only; the error and query bounds are separate statements.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.run_: For a polynomial $P$ of total degree strictly below $b^c$, the honest points and lines tables make the local corrector return the requested bit $L(P(a))$ for every seed. Assume $b\ge1$, distinct test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. The sampled outer parameter is nonzero. This is an exact completeness assertion and gives no numerical query bound; the $3c+9$ estimate is the separate statement attached to the first sentence.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalCorrection.samp: The complete seed consists of an outer slope, a nonzero field parameter, an inner correction slope, a homogeneous label and a seed for the inner low-degree test. The formal definition passes those choices to the correction procedure at the fixed target. Uniform sampling over the product makes the listed choices independent, while the two corrected reads deliberately reuse the same inner slope and label. The definition alone asserts neither correctness nor a success probability.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryLocalRowDecoding.exi: For $q>2c$, generator nodes and $r\ge1$, every received binary table has some nearby degree-$c$ polynomial whose encoding satisfies both full-label and homogeneous-label distance bounds $K_c\kappa$. Here $K_c=4(c+2)^2(112(c+2)+60)$ and $\kappa$ is rejection by the test that chooses between its two parts with a fair coin. No small-rejection condition is imposed. For large $\kappa$ the bound may exceed one, so existence then carries no useful closeness information.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryStandardLocalCorrect: Assume the correction nodes are distinct and nonzero and $U$ has total degree at most $c$. At every fixed target $u$, the corrected bit differs from $L(U(u))$ with probability at most $(c+1)\tau$, where $\tau$ is homogeneous-label distance from the received table to the encoding of $U$. The probability averages jointly over the uniform slope and homogeneous label. The statement gives no guarantee for each fixed label of an arbitrary received table.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BinaryZeroOnGridCorrection: Assume $b\ge1$, $q>2c$, generator test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. Let the target polynomial and certificate polynomial have degrees at most $D\ge cb^c$, and let the nonempty grid have size $h$ in each coordinate. Suppose $\delta_P,\delta_M$ bound the corresponding global homogeneous table errors. If the target does not vanish on the grid, rejection is at least $[(1-Dh/q)/2-\delta_P-2\delta_M-D/(q-1)]/(1+2C_c)$. The denominator is positive, but a negative numerator gives no useful rejection guarantee. Multiplying by that denominator gives (B21).
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BivariateAgreement.exists_: Assume $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, and degree-$d$ row and column polynomials whose mean errors against $f$ are both at most $\varepsilon\le1/100$. The statement constructs a polynomial within distance $4\varepsilon$ of $f$, with degree at most $d$ in each variable. Its total degree may therefore be $2d$. The row and column approximants are arbitrary; they do not need to minimize distance. Existence of the comparison polynomial is a conclusion, not a premise.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BivariateAgreementBoost.di: The comparison polynomial $P$ is supplied and has degree at most $d$ in each variable. Suppose both polynomial families approximate $f$ with mean error at most $\varepsilon$, and $P$ is already within some distance $\rho$. If $\rho+\varepsilon+2d/q\le1/3$, the conclusion improves that distance to $4\varepsilon$. The statement does not construct the initial comparison polynomial. The preceding clean-rectangle argument supplies it with $\rho\le\varepsilon+1/9$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BivariateCleanRectangle.ex: For a nonzero bivariate locator $E$ with degree at most $e$ in the first variable, take distinct selected column positions. Assume both individual degrees of $E$ are below the field size and there are more than $d+e$ positions. The result selects $d+1$ distinct columns where the specialized locator remains a nonzero polynomial. The paper applies it with $e=2d$ and $10d$ positions. Selecting the many rows of the clean rectangle is a later step.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BivariateColumnSelection.e: If the row and column families each have mean error at most $\varepsilon\le1/100$ against $f$, and $q\ge20d$, there are $10d$ distinct columns on which the two families disagree on at most a tenth of the rows. Their polynomial degree bounds are not used in this selection. The conclusion concerns discrepancy between the two approximating families, not the error of each chosen column against $f$ separately.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.BivariateCrossingSoundness: This result uses a nearest degree-$d$ polynomial for every row and every column. With $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, global errors at most $\varepsilon\le1/100$, crossing-slice errors at most $\varepsilon'$ and $5\varepsilon+\varepsilon'+2d/q<1/2$, the two values at the crossing agree. The bivariate comparison polynomial is constructed internally. The paper’s more general formulation permits arbitrary approximants away from the crossing, so this statement alone covers only its all-nearest case.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.CandidateCrossing.crossing: The row and column families have degree at most $d$ and satisfy the two global and two transverse error bounds of the crossing argument, all at most $\varepsilon$. The selected row polynomial additionally lies within $\varepsilon$ of its own row; only the selected column polynomial must be nearest. With $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, $\varepsilon\le1/100$ and $6\varepsilon+2d/q<1/2$, the crossing values agree. This is the variant needed after one column of the sampled surface is changed.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.DerivedZeroOnGrid.rejectio: Assume $b\ge1$, $q>2c$, generator test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. Let each $A_x$ have degree at most $r$ and satisfy $A_x(g(x))=A(x)$, where $A$ and the proposed certificate have degrees at most $D_1\ge cb^c$. If $A$ does not vanish on the nonempty grid, the test satisfies $(1-D_1h/q)/2\le(1+2C_c)(\kappa+2\varepsilon)+2\delta_M+D_1/(q-1)$. Here $\varepsilon$ bounds the primary table’s full-label error and $\delta_M$ bounds the certificate’s homogeneous error. Replacing the primary read changes rejection, so its $2\varepsilon$ loss receives the multiplier $1+2C_c$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.e: Put $D=cb^c$ and assume $b\ge1$, $r\ge1$, generator test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. If $q\ge10^6D^3$ and $J_c\kappa\le1/4{,}000{,}000$, one polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $D$ approximates the received points table within $S_c\kappa$ over both full labels and homogeneous labels. The lines table is arbitrary. The statement gives existence of $P$ for the analysis; the verifier does not compute it.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.q: For every seed and $r\ge1$, the complete query list has length at most $2r+2c+12$. It includes the Hadamard test on a points-table row, the inner low-degree test on the chosen line entry and the corrected comparison. The count is valid for arbitrary nodes and received tables. Distinctness, generator and field-size conditions are needed for the mathematical guarantees of those tests, not for counting the listed addresses.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.EncodedLineLowDegreeTest.t: Let $P$ have total degree strictly below $b^c$, with $b\ge1$. If the points table and all line entries are its honest encodings, every seed accepts. The test nodes only need to be distinct; the correction nodes need to be distinct and nonzero. The generator and large-field assumptions used for soundness are unnecessary here. The strict degree condition is what lets the set-multilinear encoding recover the restriction of $P$ to each line.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.GeneratorLowDegreeTest.exi: Take the first $c+1$ powers of a generator of the field’s multiplicative group and their Lagrange weights for evaluation at zero. If $q>2c$ and the rejection probability is at most $\delta<1/[2(c+2)^2]$, the function is within distance $2\delta$ of a polynomial of total degree at most $c$. The field can have any characteristic, and $c=0$ is included. This result concerns the generator-weighted test, not the version-1 unit-weight test.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.GridInterpolation.existsUn: For a finite nonempty set $H$ in a field and a function on $H^k$, exactly one polynomial has the prescribed values and degree at most $|H|-1$ in each variable. Finiteness of the ambient field is unnecessary. Nonemptiness of $H$ matters for uniqueness with this degree convention. The statement controls individual degrees; the total-degree bound $k(|H|-1)$ is established separately for the interpolant.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.GridVanishing.vanishesOn_i: Over an integral domain, vanishing on a finite nonempty grid is equivalent to existence of a polynomial $M$ of degree at most $\deg A$ with the two formal substitution identities $M(X,0)=0$ and $M(X,Z_H(X))=A(X)$. These are identities of polynomials, stronger than agreement at field points. The theorem’s conclusion does not require $M$ to be linear in its second block. The proof constructs such an $M$ from the grid decomposition; the unrestricted converse is available separately.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.exists_field_func: For a received points table with labels in $\mathcal B_r$, $r\ge1$, the result selects one field value at each point. The resulting function $g$ has encoding distance at most $28\overline e$ from the table both over all labels and over homogeneous labels, where $\overline e$ is the average Hadamard-test rejection probability. No upper bound on $\overline e$ is assumed. The selected function need not be polynomial; the inner low-degree test supplies polynomiality later.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.relativeDistance_: When $r\ge1$, encoding two functions by degree-$r$ Hadamard words divides their relative distance by two. This statement averages over all labels in $\mathcal B_r$ and only requires the coordinate map to be injective. It neither restricts the labels to homogeneous ones nor bounds a received word’s error on that subset. The homogeneous half-distance identity is a separate result, needed by the difference check.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.selfCorrect_failu: For a received word $w$ close to an additive homomorphism $\varphi$, the read $w(\Lambda+R)-w(R)$ differs from $\varphi(\Lambda)$ with probability at most $2\Delta(w,\varphi)$ over uniform $R$, for every fixed $\Lambda$. Translation preserves the uniform distribution, so no averaging over the requested label is needed. The statement works for finite additive input groups and arbitrary additive commutative output groups. It does not require the corrected value to be a field-polynomial evaluation.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.Hadamard.test_soundness: Assume $r\ge1$ and the Hadamard test rejects with probability at most $\epsilon<1/28$. One binary vector then gives an encoding within distance $\epsilon$ over all labels in $\mathcal B_r$ and within $3\epsilon$ over affine labels. The field element is recovered from that vector using the fixed coordinate isomorphism. The second distance here is affine, not homogeneous. Restricting it to homogeneous labels can double the bound, which is why the row-decoding argument keeps the two label distributions distinct.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.HadamardComposition.encode: Given $A\in F[Y]$ with $\deg A\le r$ and an affine label $L$, the composed label in $\mathcal B_r$ gives the identity $\mathcal H_r(u)(\Lambda_{A,L})=L(A(u))$ for every $u$. The coordinate isomorphism is linear over the binary field. The same label works for all $u$; it is not chosen after learning the field value. This statement concerns honest encodings. A corrupted word needs the separate two-query correction estimate.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.HadamardDerivedOracle.answ: Let $A$ have degree at most $r$, and let $L$ be an affine label. On an honest degree-$r$ Hadamard word for $u$, the two-query corrected read of the composed label equals $L(A(u))$ for every fresh label $R$. The polynomial $A$ may be nonlinear or constant. This is an exact identity on an honest word; the bound for a corrupted word requires a separate averaging argument over $R$.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.LineTableLocalCorrection.c: Each proposed line polynomial has degree at most $d$, as does the target polynomial $P$. At a fixed target, the procedure chooses a uniform slope and a uniform nonzero parameter, accepts only when the proposed line agrees with the received function there, and returns the line’s value at zero. The probability of an accepted wrong answer is at most $\Delta(f,P)+d/(q-1)$. Rejection is not counted as failure in this statement, and acceptance need not be frequent.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PointLineConstants.field_b: This arithmetic result starts from $d>0$ and $q\ge10^6d^3$. It supplies the field bounds needed for bivariate agreement, the fixed-parameter estimate and the line characterization: $q\ge1000d^3$, $q\ge3d$, $q>2d$ and $q\ge10^6$. It also gives the crossing inequality at $\varepsilon=1/100$. The assertion is about integer and rational inequalities, so it does not require $q$ to be a field cardinality until those bounds are used elsewhere.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PointLineConstants.rigidit: With $q\ge10^6$ and $\delta'\le1/4{,}000{,}000$, substitute $\varepsilon=1/100$, $\eta=2\delta'$, $\mu=4\delta'$ and $\gamma=8(4\delta'+1/q)/\varepsilon$ into the ruled-surface exceptional-event expression. The statement proves that the resulting value is strictly less than one. That is enough to ensure a successful choice of the sampled surface. The numerical bound $0.482025$ is a sharper calculation displayed in the paper, not part of this formal statement’s conclusion.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PointLineCrossing.crossing: A bivariate comparison polynomial $P$ of individual degree at most $d$ is supplied, with distance at most $\rho$ from $f$. Global row and column errors are at most $\varepsilon$, crossing-slice errors at most $\varepsilon'$, and only the two selected polynomials must be nearest. The inequality $2(\varepsilon'+\varepsilon+\rho+d/q)<1-d/q$ forces their crossing values to agree. This helper assumes the nearby polynomial; the bivariate agreement theorem constructs it in the paper’s application.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.exists_close: When every line entry is constant, there is a constant polynomial whose distance from $f$ is at most twice the whole-field test’s rejection probability. There is no lower bound on field size and no upper bound on the rejection probability. The result covers arbitrary finite dimension, including dimension zero. Its conclusion concerns approximation of the points function; it does not require all the constants supplied in the lines table to agree with one another.

A degree-$d$ line polynomial is supplied for every indexed line, without any compatibility requirement between different indices. The test samples the line parameter from the whole field. If $q\ge10^6d^3$ and rejection is at most $1/4{,}000{,}000$, a polynomial of total degree at most $d$ is within twice the rejection probability of the points function. Degree zero and dimension zero are included. The statement does not directly describe the source test that samples only nonzero parameters.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PointLineTest.rejectionAt_: Replace each line entry by a nearest polynomial of degree at most $d$ and let its mean rejection probability be $\delta'$. When $q\ge3d$, evaluation at any fixed line parameter has error at most $4\delta'$ over uniform base points and slopes. Arbitrary choices between tied nearest polynomials are allowed. The nearestness assumption matters: the conclusion is not stated for an arbitrary received lines table. The parameter is fixed before the base point and slope are sampled.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.PolynomialLine.exists_poly: Assume every restriction $t\mapsto f(u+tv)$ is a polynomial function of degree at most $d$ and the finite field has $q>2d$ elements. Then one multivariate polynomial of total degree at most $d$ represents $f$ at every point. Every base point and slope is included, including the zero slope. The coordinate set can be any finite set, so zero-dimensional spaces are allowed. No characteristic-two assumption is used.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.RuledSurface.hasLowDegreeL: The inputs are functions $f,g$ and any degree-$d$ lines table with the stated distance, endpoint, whole-test and fixed-parameter bounds $\eta,\gamma,\delta',\mu$. Assume $d>0$, $q\ge1000d^3$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/100$, the crossing inequality and $(2(\gamma+\eta)+\delta'+\mu+\gamma+2/q)/\varepsilon+\gamma<1$. Then every affine-line restriction of $g$ is exactly a degree-$d$ polynomial function. The same polynomial works at all parameters on each chosen line; a new polynomial is not chosen separately at each point.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.decode: The substitution replaces each block variable $X_{i,k}$ by $Y^{kb^i}$ and keeps coefficients fixed. Its output is a univariate polynomial, before any value of $Y$ is chosen. It is defined for arbitrary polynomials in the block variables, including polynomials that are not set-multilinear encodings. The recovery theorem and the bound on the decoded degree are separate statements. The definition only needs a commutative semiring of coefficients.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.decode_enco: If $b\ge1$ and the univariate polynomial $p$ has degree strictly below $b^c$, substituting $Y^{kb^i}$ in its set-multilinear encoding recovers $p$ as a polynomial. This is stronger than equality of evaluation functions over a finite field. The strict degree bound ensures that the $c$ base-$b$ digits preserve every exponent in the support. The result is valid for any commutative semiring of coefficients, including the finite-field setting of the paper.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.encode_inje: Two univariate polynomials of degree strictly below $b^c$ have equal set-multilinear encodings only if they are equal as formal polynomials. The assumption $b\ge1$ is required. Injectivity follows by applying the power substitution that recovers the original polynomial. No assumption on the size of the coefficient field is needed, and the result even holds over a commutative semiring. It does not assert injectivity outside the bounded-degree domain.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.SetMultilinear.eval_encode: For every $z$, evaluating the set-multilinear encoding at the power point $\Phi(z)$ gives $p(z)$, provided $b\ge1$ and $\deg p<b^c$. The result uses the same fixed polynomial $p$ for every $z$. It is an evaluation consequence of polynomial recovery, so it does not identify arbitrary polynomials merely from their values over a finite field. No field-size hypothesis is needed, and the statement is valid over a commutative semiring.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.StandardLocalCorrection.fa: For a polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $c$, assume the powers of the correction element give $c+1$ distinct nonzero nodes. The interpolated value at any fixed target $u$ differs from $P(u)$ with probability at most $(c+1)\Delta(f,P)$ over the uniform slope. No small-error assumption or additional field-size bound is required. The estimate is pointwise in the target; the queried points are individually uniform even though they need not be independent.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAlgebra.sub_cube: Assume the field has characteristic two and both proposed colours satisfy $u^3=v^3=1$. Then $(u-v)^3=1$ is equivalent to $u\ne v$. The statement does not need finiteness of the field or a chosen primitive cube root. That root is used elsewhere to identify the three possible colours. The vertex equations remain necessary: the edge equation alone does not force an arbitrary assignment to use only three colours.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorAmplifiedVerifie: This is the result for the particular amplified graph verifier. Its chosen repetition count $R$ is positive, the query bound is $187R$, and both coefficients of the exact logarithmic randomness formula are multiplied by $R$. The proof-address polynomial is unchanged. Yes-instances retain perfect completeness and every proof for a no-instance has acceptance probability at most $1/2$. The result does not itself state the general repetition lemma for arbitrary verifiers or arbitrary gaps.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorCanonicalVerifie: This statement collects the mathematical guarantees of the base graph verifier: at most $187$ queried bits, exactly $32{,}000{,}000\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+32{,}000{,}000$ fair bits, and all proof addresses below $(4(n+1))^{4{,}224{,}000}$. It has perfect completeness and rejects every proof for a non-three-colourable graph with probability at least $g_4/16$. It applies to every binary input under the fixed graph-decoding convention. Polynomial running time is not part of this statement.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorFinalAssembly.of: This assembly result assumes polynomial running time for the fixed amplified graph-verifier algorithm. It then uses the constructed NP reduction and the verifier’s established mathematical guarantees to obtain the full PCP conclusion for every NP language. The extra runtime premise is supplied by Section 3.9 and is discharged in the final theorem. Its conclusion includes an exact logarithmic randomness formula and a polynomial bound on every reachable proof address; it is not limited to completeness and soundness alone.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorGrid.colorable_i: The graph has the grid points as vertices, the field has characteristic two, and a primitive cube root of unity is supplied. Three-colourability is equivalent to existence of a polynomial $P$ of total degree at most $m(h-1)$ for which the vertex and edge constraints vanish on their grids. The edge constraint uses the input’s adjacency extension and the actual difference polynomial $P(X)-P(Y)$. This is an existence theorem; the statement for any fixed $P$ is separate.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.colorab: The formal statement assembles the complete algebraic soundness argument. Under the field, grid, degree and node assumptions of Theorem 3.8, a received proof with rejection probability below $g_c$ forces the graph to be three-colourable. The proof chooses four nearby polynomials from the four low-degree tests, identifies the difference polynomial, and uses both zero-on-grid checks to obtain the vertex and edge constraints. No nearby polynomials are supplied as hypotheses.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.exists_: Assume characteristic two, a primitive cube root of unity, a nonempty grid, distinct test nodes and distinct nonzero correction nodes. If $5m(h-1)<b^c$, every three-colourable grid graph has an eight-table proof accepted on every seed. The proof uses a colouring extension and two vanishing certificates, together with their encoded line restrictions. This is perfect completeness for the algebraic verifier; converting its samples to fair bits and implementing it are later steps.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.queries: For each fixed seed, the complete seven-check query list contains at most $20c+107$ addresses. The bound includes both physical queries in every self-corrected read and is independent of the graph size. Repeated addresses are still counted as entries of the list. This statement only bounds the list’s length. The separate agreement-of-verdicts result shows that equality of the answers at those addresses is enough to determine the verifier’s verdict.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.rejecti: Assume $c,b,h\ge1$, characteristic two, a primitive cube root of unity and the required generator and correction nodes. With $D=cb^c$, the field bounds are $q\ge10^6D^3$ and $q\ge100Dh$, and the grid degree satisfies $m(h-1)\le D$. Then every received proof for a non-three-colourable grid graph is rejected with probability at least $g_c$. The quantifier is over arbitrary tables, including tables that encode no polynomial.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.ThreeColorVerifier.test_co: Fix the graph, parameters and a complete seven-check seed. If two received proofs agree at every address on the complete query list, they produce the same verdict. The proofs need not encode polynomials, and the node choices need not satisfy the conditions used for completeness or soundness. This is the dependency statement that lets a finite query list represent the actual verifier, separately from the numerical bound on its length.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.WeightedConstraint.correct: For nonzero nodes $a_1,\ldots,a_n$, form the weighted prediction and take its plurality over uniform slopes at each point. If the original constraint rejection probability $\delta$ satisfies $(2n^2+3n)\delta<1$, this corrected function satisfies every constraint exactly. The nodes may repeat and weights may vanish. The conclusion is exact consistency, not the separate distance estimate $\Delta(f,g)\le2\delta$. Polynomiality follows only after an exact characterization of the chosen constraints is applied.
notes.PCP.Algebraic.eval_zero_agreement_le: For a nonzero polynomial $P$ over a finite field of size $q$, the fraction of zeros on the whole affine space is at most $\deg P/q$. No assumption $\deg P<q$ is needed, although the bound may then give no information. If an upper bound $d$ on the degree is supplied, the paper’s estimate $d/q$ follows. The result includes zero-dimensional affine space.
notes.PCP.Lang.ThreeColorRuntime.polyTimeAlg: The result asserts polynomial running time for the fixed amplified verifier’s next-step algorithm on the concrete multi-stack machine model. Its input consists of the original binary input, the random string and the answer history, with fixed encodings; its output is a verdict or a binary proof address. The proof combines the seven-check program’s correctness and cost bounds with the repetition implementation. Equality with the intended query tree is a separate condition in the final PCP theorem.
notes.PCP.Machine.NPTableau.exists_accepts_iff: For a supplied polynomial-time witness checker and witness-length polynomial, there is an accepting bounded tableau exactly when some witness within the bound is accepted. The assignment contains the witness and all bounded configurations. Its acceptance condition fixes the initial row, every transition and the final accepting row. The statement allows witnesses of every length up to the bound, including zero. It is a semantic equivalence; locality and the running time of the later graph reduction are separate results.
notes.PCP.QueryTree.ofStep: The construction takes a next-step procedure, the answers already received and a remaining query budget. A verdict becomes a leaf. A query with positive budget creates two continuations, one for each possible answer, and reduces the budget by one. A query at budget zero becomes rejection. Thus the tree makes at most the prescribed number of queries; constructing this mathematical tree alone says nothing about the time needed to compute each next step.
notes.PCP.Reduction.FiniteDomainConstraints.sa: Each source symbol is represented by a Boolean block with exactly one true bit. The translated system contains constraints enforcing that validity condition and constraints expressing the original relations on the decoded symbols. A satisfying Boolean assignment exists exactly when the source constraint system is satisfiable. The statement is independent of whether alphabet size and arity grow with the input; those sizes must later be fixed to obtain the polynomial resource bounds used by the reduction.
notes.PCP.Reduction.NAEThreeColor.colorable_if: The graph contains a palette triangle, adjacent complementary vertices for each Boolean variable and a triangle for each NAE clause. A three-colouring exists exactly when there is a Boolean assignment satisfying every NAE clause. Constants are interpreted using the palette vertices. The equivalence permits an arbitrary permutation of the three colours; relabelling the palette recovers the Boolean assignment. This statement establishes satisfiability preservation, while graph encoding and construction cost are treated separately.
notes.PCP.Reduction.NPThreeColorRuntime.of_inN: For every language with a polynomial-time bounded witness checker, the statement supplies a map to encoded graphs and a program computing it. A single polynomial bounds the output length, and fixed constants $C,e$ bound charged cost by $C(|x|+1)^e$ on every input. The resulting graph is three-colourable exactly when the input is in the language. These objects and bounds are chosen before the input, so the result is a uniform reduction.
notes.PCP.ReferenceNP.inNP_iff_mem: The statement identifies two precise definitions of NP: polynomially bounded witnesses checked in the project’s deterministic multi-stack model, and the reference nondeterministic-machine class. It proves an equivalence for every language, with no machine-simulation or cost assumption left to supply. The individual simulations are imported by this source file. This result connects the concrete machine model used by the forward and reverse PCP theorems with the reference complexity class.
notes.PCP.Verifier.ImplementedBy: An implementation is tied to a verifier by requiring equality of their complete bounded query trees on every input and seed. This includes the addresses and both possible answer branches. The condition imposes no running-time bound and does not independently require the next-step procedure to issue a verdict before exhausting the query budget. A further query at depth zero is interpreted as rejection. Polynomial running time is an additional mathematical condition.
notes.PCP.np_subset_pcp: For each language in NP, one verifier and one polynomial-time implementation are chosen independently of the input. Its randomness is exactly $\alpha\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil+\beta$, its query bound is a fixed constant, and every reachable proof address is below a fixed polynomial in $n$. Every yes-instance has one proof accepted on every seed; every proof for a no-instance is accepted on at most half the seeds. The machine model is the concrete model described in Section 2.3.
notes.PCP.pcp_subset_np_concrete: The assumptions are a polynomial-time implementation, an exact logarithmic randomness formula, a polynomial bound on all reachable proof addresses, perfect completeness and soundness error $1/2$. Under these conditions the language belongs to the concrete NP class. A finite proof prefix is enough as a witness because no query leaves it. The number of seeds is polynomial, so the witness checker can simulate every seed and accept exactly when all of them accept.
